titel: The king's word and the council's (1415)
autor: Sigismund's chancery; the lords of Bohemia and Moravia; the Council of Constance
quelle: F. Palacký, Documenta Mag. Joannis Hus (Prague: Tempský, 1869), nos. 70, 74 and 81, pp. 543–572. Internet Archive, documentamagjoa00palagoog (Google scan). Public domain.
hinweis: Three documents on the safe conduct and the sentence, all from Palacký's Documenta: the king's revocation of the safe conducts after the pope's flight, the Czech petition of 250 Bohemian and Moravian lords, and the council's letter to Bohemia after the burning. Read against the page images; Palacký's Latin and old Czech spelling are kept. The council's decrees themselves (Haec sancta, the sentence of 6 July) are in the module 'The council's decrees' (Decr.). Cuts are marked […]. The English is this site's working translation (CC0).

sections.titel: The king revokes the safe conducts (8 April 1415)
sections.blurb: After the pope's flight, with the council's consent, Sigismund quashes every safe conduct he has given at Constance.

units.titel: The king revokes every safe conduct
units.orig: Sigismundus dei gratia Romanorum rex semper Augustus ac Hungariae, Dalmatiae, Croatiae &c. rex. Universis et singulis hanc nostrae declarationis paginam inspecturis pateat evidenter, [...] Cum igitur quampluribus in hoc felici Constantiensi concilio existentibus Nostrae Majestatis salvorum conductuum literas dederimus gratiose, ipsique dictas literas, ut nobis innotuit relatione fide digna, cautulose reservant, quod ex certis indiciis, praesentibus non reserandis, in aliquorum verisimiliter vergere dispendium formidantur: quapropter, de consensu et voluntate hujus sacratissimi concilii, omnes et singulos salvos conductus, quibuscunque, cujuscunque conditionis, gradus, eminentiae existant, per nos datos et concessos in hac civitate Constantiensi, quorum quid dum (sic) ipsorum impetrantes usi sunt, sicque detinentes, ex certis causis animum nostrum moventibus cassamus, annullamus et revocamus tenore praesentium, nullos, cassos et revocatos tenore praesentium declaramus, praesentium sub nostri regalis sigilli impressione testimonio literarum. Dat. Constantiae anno domini MCCCCXV, VIII die mensis Aprilis, regnorum nostrorum Hungariae XXXVIII, Romanorum vero quinto. Ad mandatum domini regis: Joannes de Strigonio &c. Et nos Joannes archiepiscopus Rigensis et Nicolaus episcopus Merseburgensis, deputati per nationem Germanicam, similiter revocamus omnes salvos conductus, ut supra in literis regalibus continetur.
units.en: Sigismund, by the grace of God king of the Romans, ever augustus, and king of Hungary, Dalmatia, Croatia etc. To all and each who shall see this page of our declaration, let it be plainly known [...]. Since, then, we have graciously given letters of safe conduct of our Majesty to very many who are in this happy Council of Constance, and they, as we have learned from trustworthy report, keep the said letters carefully, which from certain signs, not to be disclosed at present, are feared likely to turn to the harm of some: therefore, with the consent and will of this most holy council, all and each of the safe conducts given and granted by us in this city of Constance to anyone, of whatever condition, rank or eminence they be, which those who obtained them have used and so hold, we, for certain causes that move our mind, quash, annul and revoke by the tenor of these presents, and declare them null, quashed and revoked by the tenor of these presents, in witness whereof these letters are sealed with our royal seal. Given at Constance in the year of the Lord 1415, on the eighth day of the month of April, in the thirty-eighth year of our reign in Hungary, and the fifth as king of the Romans. By order of the lord king: John of Esztergom etc. And we, John archbishop of Riga and Nicholas bishop of Merseburg, deputed by the German nation, likewise revoke all safe conducts, as is contained above in the royal letters.
units.note: 8 April 1415, less than three weeks after John XXIII's flight, when the council feared that the pope's friends would use their safe conducts to leave or to plot. The revocation covers conducts given 'in this city of Constance'; Hus's letter had been given at Speyer and he had been in prison for four months. It was not made against him, but it shows what a king's safe conduct was worth to a king and a council in 1415 (Mlad. Journey [1]). Palacký printed it from a faulty Prague copy ('mendose scripto').

sections.blurb: Two hundred and fifty lords, knights and squires of Bohemia and Moravia write to Sigismund in Czech: Hus was seized under your safe conduct; release him, or no one will trust your safe conducts again.

units.orig: Najjasnějšiemu kniežeti, panu Sigismundowi Římskému a Uherskému &c. králi, pánu našemu milostiwému: my w dole psaní páni, rytieři a panoše země České i Morawské wzkazujem službu swú wěrnú. Jakož papež Jan třimedcietmý lóni rozeslal po wšem křesťanstwí swé bully a listy, klada w nich a ohlašuje obecné swolánie do Konstancie, pro sjednánie wiery křesťanské a wšech jiných roztržení, dáwaje těmi listy a bullami wšem swój jistý a bezpečný gleit a jistotu plnú a swobodu, aby každý dobrý i zlý, křesťan i kacieř, kteréhožkoliwěk řádu, bezpečně mohl přijeti i otjeti k tomu i od toho swolánie: [...] Tu poctiwý muž a kazatel wěrný slowa božieho mistr Jan Hus jel jest odsad k tomu swolánie dobrowolně, pro křiwé narčenie, kteréž jest jemu bez winy, a skrze to wšie České koruně a jazyku připisowáno. [...] A Twá Milost přes to wšechno mnohými pány swými jeho jest obeslala, aby wždy přijel k tomu sboru, a k tomu i list swój gleitowní a bezpečenstwie jemu poslala; a ten jest zde po wší zemi České i Morawské rozhlášen i rozepsán. Tu když jest do Konstancie přijel, jat jest w Twém gleitu a w wězenie w těžké wsazen, beze wší zpráwy a slyšení, proti prawdě a řádu i gleitu Twú Milostí wydanému.
units.en: To the most illustrious prince, the lord Sigismund, king of the Romans and of Hungary etc., our gracious lord: we, the lords, knights and squires of the land of Bohemia and of Moravia written below, send our faithful service. Pope John the Twenty-third last year sent his bulls and letters throughout Christendom, announcing in them a general assembly at Constance for the uniting of the Christian faith and of all other divisions, and giving by these letters and bulls to all his sure and safe conduct and full assurance and freedom, so that everyone, good and bad, Christian and heretic, of whatever order, might safely come to that assembly and go from it: [...] Then the honest man and faithful preacher of the word of God, Master Jan Hus, went from here to that assembly of his own free will, because of the false accusation that was laid on him without guilt, and through him on the whole Bohemian crown and tongue. [...] And your Grace besides all this sent many of your lords to him, that he should by all means come to that council, and moreover sent him your letter of safe conduct and security; and it has been proclaimed and copied here throughout all the land of Bohemia and Moravia. When he came to Constance, he was seized under your safe conduct and put in harsh prison, without any process or hearing, against truth and order and the safe conduct your Grace issued.
units.note: Prague, 12 May 1415, in Czech. The lords argue from two promises: the pope's bulls, which promised safe passage to 'good and bad, Christian and heretic', and the king's letter, which 'has been proclaimed and copied throughout all the land'. A note in the Mladoňovice manuscript, printed by Palacký, records that the letter bore 250 seals and was read in Latin to the deputies of the four nations on 12 June in the Franciscan refectory, where Páleč protested that 'no mention was made of our lord the king'.

units.titel: 'Many would have cause to fear your Grace's safe conducts'
units.orig: A o to zde i jinde mezi kniežaty, pány, rytieři i panošemi, chudými i bohatými, weliké řeči jdú, že papež tak proti swým listóm i bullám, proti řádu i prawdě, a proti gleitu TMti učinil, a mistra Jana Husi, muže dáli bóh sprawedliwého, bez winy, beze wšeho slyšenie a dówodu prawého, w wězenie wsadil, nám i wšie České zemi i jazyku na hanbu a na potupenie. Protož TMt rač to ještě milostiwě opatřiti, jako král a pán a dědic nápadný koruny České, poněwadž kacieři potupení do Konstancie ot Řehoře i ot Benedikta poslaní, měli sú a mají pokoj a bezpečenstwí, a již také papež, nechaw tu mistra Jana Husi, pryč jest jel a w Twé moci jeho tu ostawil: aby mistr Jan Hus, již dosti bez winy trpěw, byl propuštěn a wyswobozen, a wiece mocí a bez řádu nebyl žalařowán, na hanbu a na potupenie wšemu jazyku Českému, tak jakož TMt jej obeslala a bezpečně gleitowala. Neb jinak napřed TMti, a potom wšie České koruně bylby weliký úraz skrze také neřádné a nesprawedliwé wězenie člowěka sprawedliwého, jenž jest, jakož slyšíme, již w Twé moci i w Twém městě jat, maje Twé sliby i listy gleitownie; a mnohým bylaby příčina, žeby sě TMti gleitów lekali; jakož již o to řeči weliké jdú, kteréž o TMti nerádi slyšíme. [...] Psán w Praze, léta od božieho narozenie tisícieho čtrstého patnáctého, tu neděli po božím wstúpení, pod našimi pečetmi wespod přitištěnými &c.
units.en: And about this, here and elsewhere, among princes, lords, knights and squires, poor and rich, there is great talk that the pope has acted so against his own letters and bulls, against order and truth, and against your Grace's safe conduct, and has put Master Jan Hus, a man, God willing, just, without guilt, without any hearing and proper proof, in prison, to the shame and disgrace of us and of the whole Bohemian land and tongue. Therefore may your Grace be pleased still graciously to see to it, as king and lord and heir apparent of the crown of Bohemia, since the condemned heretics sent to Constance by Gregory and by Benedict have had and still have peace and safety, and since the pope too, leaving Master Jan Hus there, has gone away and left him there in your power: that Master Jan Hus, who has already suffered enough without guilt, be released and set free, and no longer be imprisoned by force and without order, to the shame and disgrace of the whole Bohemian tongue, as your Grace summoned him and gave him safe conduct. For otherwise great harm would come, first to your Grace, and then to the whole Bohemian crown, from such disorderly and unjust imprisonment of a just man, who, as we hear, has been seized in your power and in your city while holding your promises and letters of safe conduct; and many would have cause to fear your Grace's safe conducts, as there is already great talk of it, which we do not gladly hear of your Grace. [...] Written at Prague in the year of God's birth one thousand four hundred and fifteen, on the Sunday after the Ascension of the Lord, under our seals pressed below, etc.
units.note: The argument is political as much as legal: the rival popes' envoys, 'condemned heretics' in the council's own eyes, came and went safely; a king whose safe conducts are not kept will find no one to trust them. The cut asks the king to let Hus return 'as freely as he came' for the sake of God's truth, the king's good name and the peace of Bohemia. The Sunday after the Ascension in 1415 was 12 May.

sections.blurb: Three weeks after the burning, the council tells the lords and the towns of Prague why Hus died, and threatens anyone who defends him.

units.titel: The council explains itself to Bohemia
units.orig: Sacrosancta synodus Constantiensis, universalem dei ecclesiam repraesentans, in spiritu sancto legitime congregata, viris magnificis ac spectabilibus, universis nobilibus baronibus et proceribus regni Bohemiae, (et sapientibus viris, magistris civium, scabinis et ceteris civibus majoris, minoris et novae civitatis Pragensis) salutem in domino! [...] Scitote autem, viri nobiles (prudentes), nos eundem Joannem Hus primo, ex reverendissimis dominis cardinalibus, ex praelatorum ac magistrorum excellentissimorum quam pluribus examini suo deputatis, demum data sibi pluries publica audientia, serenissimo Romanorum semper Augusto ac Ungariae &c. rege assistente, quae quemadmodum intelligeret, auscultasse; denique cum obstinatissimus in erroribus existeret, ne animae periculum suae pateretur, utque omnibus de nostra diligentia gravitateque constaret, curavimus ipsum persaepe evocare et coram quam pluribus praelatis, doctoribus et magistris suae mentis sententias manifestare defensionesque proferre; multa autem penitus absurda et a fide discrepantia se credere confessus est. Eundem tamen, ut resipisceret, caritative, quanto potuimus studio monuimus, sed nec profuit. Quippe non satis dici posset, quantum et publice privatimque, ut se emendare vellet, conati sumus. Quo in casu clementer agere volebamus, cupientes vitam potius, quam mortem amplecti peccatoris; sed nec etiam proficere valuimus. Quin imo continuo obstinatior in opinionibus ac perversior diabolica instigatione exstitit. Itaque res se habet, ut in apertissima heresi ac intolerabili deprehensus et convictus, juris censurae penitus relinqueretur, et ob id in publica nostri concilii sessione damnatus ac demum degradatus, supplicio ultimo per curiam secularem exstitit judicatus.
units.en: The holy synod of Constance, representing the universal Church of God, lawfully gathered in the Holy Spirit, to the magnificent and distinguished men, all the noble barons and magnates of the kingdom of Bohemia (and to the wise men, the burgomasters, aldermen and other citizens of the Old, Lesser and New Town of Prague), greeting in the Lord! [...] Know then, noble (and prudent) men, that we first heard the same John Hus through the most reverend lord cardinals and through very many most excellent prelates and masters deputed to examine him, and then, when he had been given a public hearing several times, in the presence of the most serene king of the Romans, ever augustus, and of Hungary etc., listened to what he understood and how; and at last, since he was most obstinate in his errors, so that he should not put his soul in peril, and so that our diligence and gravity should be clear to all, we took care to call him very often and have him set out the opinions of his mind and bring forward his defences before very many prelates, doctors and masters; and he confessed that he believed many things wholly absurd and at variance with the faith. Yet we admonished him in charity, with all the zeal we could, to come to his senses, but it did no good. Indeed it could not be said enough how much we tried, publicly and privately, to make him willing to amend. In that case we wished to act mercifully, desiring rather the life than the death of the sinner; but we could not prevail. On the contrary, he became continually more obstinate in his opinions and more perverse at the devil's instigation. And so it came about that, caught and convicted in most open and intolerable heresy, he was left wholly to the censure of the law, and for that reason, condemned in a public session of our council and finally degraded, he was judged to the last punishment by the secular court.
units.note: Constance, 26 July 1415, three weeks after the burning, under the seals of the presidents of the four nations. The council's account of the same months as Mladoňovice's (Mlad. Hearings [1], Mlad. Sentence [1]): examined, heard publicly in the king's presence, admonished in charity, obstinate. It does not mention the safe conduct. The cut recalls Wyclif's condemnation at Oxford, Prague and Rome, and the council's order to dig up his bones.

units.orig: Haec perscribimus, viri prudentissimi, ut, quod nos indefesse egimus, vos etiam, quos percepimus hujus haeresis periculosissimae oppugnatores, ad ejusdem exstirpationem non solum opportune, sed celeriter intendatis, atque serenissimum regem vestrum Christianissimum piissimumque, nostrorum etiam conatuum promtissimum et efficacissimum, ut audimus, imitatorem ad solita suffragia excitetis. [...] Ne igitur tanta nota irrigemur, o viri optimi! ita et vos hortamur, quantumcumque valemus per viscera misericordiae Jesu Christi obtestamur, ut homines pestiferos, doctrinam Wiclef et Hus ejus sectatoris haereticorum damnatorum seminantes, praedicare et dogmatisare in vestris civitatibus ac partibus, quantum in vobis fuerit, non admittatis, ut labes illa pessima ab ipsius regni finibus penitus exstirpetur; scientes, si qui ausu temerario hanc nostram sententiam deo gratissimam totique christiano populo salutarem quoquomodo impugnare tentaverint, ac in eadem damnatissima haeresi perstiterint, aut in ea persistentes juverint quomodolibet vel defenderint, ultra divinam vindictam, quam debent verisimiliter exspectare, nos in eosdem debito modo juxta canonicas sanctiones processuros, ut talium correctio aliis transeat merito in exemplum. Datum Constantiae, anno domini MoCCCCXVo, indictione octava, die XXVI mensis Julii, sub appensione sigillorum praesidentium quatuor nationum.
units.en: We write this, most prudent men, so that you too, whom we have learned to be opponents of this most dangerous heresy, may apply yourselves to its extirpation, as we have tirelessly done, not only at the right time but speedily, and rouse your most serene king, most Christian and most pious, and, as we hear, a most ready and effective imitator of our efforts, to his accustomed help. [...] Lest, then, we be stained with so great a mark, O best of men, we exhort you, and adjure you as far as we can by the bowels of the mercy of Jesus Christ, not to allow, as far as it lies with you, pestilent men who sow the teaching of the condemned heretics Wyclif and Hus his follower to preach and teach in your cities and lands, so that this worst of blemishes may be wholly rooted out from the borders of the kingdom; knowing that if any with rash daring try in any way to attack this sentence of ours, most pleasing to God and salutary to all the Christian people, and persist in that most damned heresy, or help or defend in any way those who persist in it, then, beyond the divine vengeance they must surely expect, we shall proceed against them in due manner according to the canonical sanctions, so that their correction may rightly serve as an example to others. Given at Constance in the year of the Lord 1415, in the eighth indiction, on the twenty-sixth day of the month of July, under the seals of the presidents of the four nations.
units.note: 'Your most serene king' is Wenceslas IV of Bohemia, not Sigismund. The letter was sent to the lords and to the three towns of Prague; a version for the archbishop and clergy of Prague added an order under penalty of law. The answer came on 2 September: a protest sealed by some 450 lords of Bohemia and Moravia (planned module 'lords').
